item.research_question: How do the type and number of elements in Ni-based single-phase equiatomic alloys affect their electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, particularly regarding the role of chemical and magnetic disorder?
item.material_system: Eight Ni-based FCC equiatomic alloys: elemental Ni, NiCo, NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr, NiCoFeCrMn, and NiCoFeCrPd
item.processing_route: Arc-melting of pure elemental metals (>99.9% pure) followed by five flips and re-melts, drop-casting into a copper mold, and conversion to single crystals or polycrystalline rods via optical floating zone furnace; samples cut to ~1 × 1 × 10 mm3 and electrolytically polished
item.test_conditions: Electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity measured from 4 to 300 K; magnetization measured in magnetic fields up to 4 T from 4 to 300 K
key_findings: Resistivities of alloys containing Cr (e.g., NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr) are about one order of magnitude larger than those without Cr (e.g., NiCoFe, NiFe).
The residual resistivity does not strongly correlate with the number of elements; the addition of Cr rapidly increases resistivity while Co has limited effects.
Thermal conductivities of the alloys are largely lower than pure metals primarily because high electrical resistivity suppresses the electronic thermal conductivity.
In concentrated alloys, lattice thermal conductivity (κg) dominates at low temperatures and is comparable to electronic thermal conductivity (κe) at room temperature.
The NiCoFeCrMn alloy exhibits a resistivity minimum at ~25 K, suggesting Kondo-like behavior or a spin glass transition.
NiCoCr is paramagnetic above 4 K, while NiCoFeCr has a Curie temperature (Tc) of ~120 K.
The addition of Cr significantly reduces magnetization due to magnetic cancellation, as Cr moments are anti-parallel to Ni, Co, and Fe moments.
item.mechanism: High residual resistivity in alloys containing Cr and Mn is strongly attributed to magnetic disorder, where the presence of antiferromagnetically coupled elements (Cr, Mn) alongside ferromagnetically coupled elements (Ni, Co, Fe) creates strong scattering potentials for both spin-up and spin-down electrons, shortening the electron mean-free-path.
item.limitations: The KKR-CPA calculations neglect displacement fluctuations, which may contribute to residual resistivity, particularly in alloys with large atomic size mismatches like NiCoFeCrPd.
item.future_work: Further studies are needed to investigate the origin of the finite positive TCR at low temperatures in NiCoCr, and additional experiments (ac susceptibility, heat capacity, neutron scattering) are required to conclusively determine the nature of the transition near 25 K in NiCoFeCrMn.
quotes: The scattering of electrons is significantly increased due to the chemical (especially magnetic) disorder.
Thermal conductivities of the alloys are largely lower than pure metals, primarily because the high electrical resistivity suppresses the electronic thermal conductivity.
The high residual resistivity of the alloys containing Cr and Mn is strongly attributed to the magnetic disorder.
